question: What is the electrical system voltage, and what supplies it?

options.text: 28-volt direct-current system, powered by an engine-driven 60-amp alternator and a battery
14-volt direct-current system, powered by a generator
115-volt alternating-current system
28-volt system powered solely by the battery, with no alternator

explanation: Electrical energy is supplied by a 28-volt, direct-current system powered by an engine-driven, 60-amp alternator and a battery.

question: What battery capacities are mentioned for the 24-volt battery, and where is it located?

options.text: 35-amp hour, in the baggage compartment
14-amp hour (or 17-amp hour if installed), on the right forward side of the firewall
7-amp hour, under the pilot's seat
60-amp hour, behind the instrument panel

explanation: The 24-volt battery is a 14-amp hour battery (or 17-amp hour, if installed), located on the right forward side of the firewall.

question: Which circuits remain powered even when the master switch is off?

options.text: The navigation lights and landing light
The entire avionics stack
The engine ignition system, clock, and flight hour recorder
The wing flap motor

explanation: The master switch controls power to all circuits except the engine ignition system, clock, or flight hour recorder (if installed) — the flight hour recorder is powered through an oil pressure switch, and the clock is powered at all times.

question: What are the two halves of the split-rocker master switch labeled, and what does each control?

options.text: ON controls the battery; OFF controls the alternator
MAIN controls the alternator; AUX controls the battery
BAT controls only the starter; ALT controls all other electrical power
BAT controls all electrical power; ALT controls the alternator

explanation: The right half of the master switch, labeled BAT, controls all electrical power to the airplane; the left half, labeled ALT, controls the alternator.

question: What happens if the airplane continues to operate with the ALT side of the master switch OFF?

options.text: Battery power will reduce enough to open the battery contactor and prevent alternator restart
The alternator will overcharge the battery
Nothing changes; the alternator continues charging normally
The ammeter will show a permanent full charge

explanation: With the ALT switch off, the entire electrical load is placed on the battery; continued operation will reduce battery power low enough to open the battery contactor, remove power from the alternator field, and prevent alternator restart.

question: What does the ammeter indicate when the alternator is not functioning or the electrical load exceeds alternator output?

options.text: The bus voltage in volts
The battery discharge rate
The alternator field current only
It reads zero regardless of load

explanation: If the alternator is not functioning, or the electrical load exceeds the alternator's output, the ammeter indicates the battery discharge rate rather than a charging rate.

question: What two components make up the over-voltage protection system, and what is the warning light labeled?

options.text: A circuit breaker and a green warning light labeled ALT FAIL
A fuse and an amber light labeled LOW VOLTS
An over-voltage sensor and a red warning light labeled HIGH VOLTAGE
A relay and a blue light labeled OVER AMP

explanation: The over-voltage protection system consists of an over-voltage sensor behind the instrument panel and a red warning light, labeled HIGH VOLTAGE, under the ammeter.

question: How can the HIGH VOLTAGE warning light be tested?

options.text: By turning off the entire master switch
By pulling the AVIONICS circuit breaker
There is no way to test this light in flight
By momentarily turning off the ALT portion of the master switch while leaving the BAT portion on

explanation: The warning light may be tested by momentarily turning off the ALT portion of the master switch and leaving the BAT portion turned on.

question: What type of circuit breakers protect most of the electrical circuits, and where are they mounted?

options.text: Push-to-reset breakers, mounted under the engine controls on the instrument panel
Pull-to-reset fuses, mounted behind the pilot's seat
Automatic resetting breakers, mounted in the tailcone
Thermal fuses, mounted in the wing root

explanation: Most electrical circuits are protected by push-to-reset circuit breakers mounted under the engine controls on the instrument panel.

question: Which circuits are protected by fuses rather than circuit breakers?

options.text: The landing light and navigation light circuits
The battery contactor closing circuit, clock circuit, and flight hour recorder circuit
The wing flap motor circuit
All avionics circuits

explanation: Circuits not protected by circuit breakers — the battery contactor closing (external power) circuit, clock circuit, and flight hour recorder circuit — are protected by fuses mounted adjacent to the battery.

question: Before connecting an external power source to the ground service plug receptacle, what should the pilot do with the master switch?

options.text: Leave the master switch OFF until the external power is connected and stable
Cycle the master switch rapidly several times
Turn the master switch ON to allow the battery to absorb transient voltages
Remove the battery entirely before connecting external power

explanation: Just before connecting an external power source, the master switch should be turned ON so the battery can absorb transient voltages that might otherwise damage the transistors in the electronic equipment.

question: Where are the conventional navigation lights located?

options.text: On the nose cowl and the tail cone
Only on the left wing tip
On the belly of the fuselage
On the wing tips and the top of the rudder

explanation: Conventional navigation lights are located on the wing tips and top of the rudder.

question: Why should the flashing beacon not be used when flying through clouds or overcast at night?

options.text: The reflected flashing light can produce vertigo and loss of orientation
It drains the battery excessively
It interferes with the ammeter reading
It is required to be off by regulation above 10,000 feet

explanation: The flashing beacon should not be used in clouds or overcast because the flashing light reflected from water droplets or particles, particularly at night, can produce vertigo and loss of orientation.

question: What do the two concentric rheostat knobs labeled PANEL LT and RADIO LT control?

options.text: Cabin temperature and defrost airflow
The intensity of flood lighting and integral lighting respectively
Navigation light and beacon brightness
Fuel quantity indicator backlighting only

explanation: The two concentric rheostat knobs, labeled PANEL LT and RADIO LT, control the intensity of both flood lighting and integral lighting respectively.

question: What is the most probable cause of a lighting system failure, and what should be checked if a light fails to illuminate?

options.text: A dead battery; check the ammeter
Low oil pressure; check the oil gage
A burned out bulb; check the appropriate circuit breaker
A stuck rheostat; replace the entire panel

explanation: The most probable cause of a light failure is a burned out bulb; if a light fails to illuminate when turned on, the appropriate circuit breaker should be checked.

question: If a circuit breaker opens a second time after being reset once, what should the pilot do?

options.text: Reset it repeatedly until it holds
Bypass it with the external power receptacle
Reset it, then immediately turn off the master switch
Do not reset it again

explanation: If the circuit breaker opens again after being reset once, it should not be reset again — this indicates a real fault rather than a transient.
